title: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: wherever the shell is but a single unit or single chamber, its form may be explained in general by the laws of surface tension: the assumption being that the little mass of protoplasm which makes the simple shell behaves as a _fluid drop_, the form of which is perpetuated when the protoplasm acquires its solid covering.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Foraminiferal shells as fluid drops”. Scope: unilocular Foraminifera (e.g. Orbulina, Lagena)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shell geometry is measurable and equilibrium models are available, but translating Thompson's fluid-drop language into boundary conditions requires interpretation. Existing images can test shape compatibility, not cleanly identify surface tension as the cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Segment unilocular shells in 3D, estimate their curvature and departures from constant-mean-curvature equilibrium shapes, and compare fits with constrained surface-tension models. Systematic agreement would support the proposed physical explanation; large structured departures would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Static shell shape does not directly measure protoplasmic tension or conditions at solidification.

Open 3D coverage of unilocular taxa is sparse.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.35
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data existence: 0.5
data adequacy: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Drop equilibrium is a standard geometric target, and planktonic unilocular tests are already imaged and measured at scale. Those collections barely cover the lagenid shapes Thompson used as the harder cases, and a good geometric fit still leaves calcification timing unmeasured. The comparison can be run on existing images for the planktonic subset within weeks, which is a partial test of the stated scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit outlines and micro-CT surfaces of unilocular tests (Orbulina, Lagena and similar genera) to constant-mean-curvature and sessile-drop profiles, and compare residual error with non-equilibrium shape models. A systematically smaller residual for drop profiles would support the claim; structured residuals concentrated in the neck or aperture would refute a pure fluid-drop equilibrium.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Open 3D coverage is dominated by planktonic Orbulina and Globigerina, while flask-shaped lagenids are mostly represented by plates and SEM images.

A sphere fits many simple generative models, so agreement for Orbulina alone is weak evidence that surface tension set the shape.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.62
